title: Container Won't Start: Port Already Allocated
intro: Running 'docker run -d -p 8080:3000 myapp:v2' fails immediately with: 'Bind for 0.0.0.0:8080 failed: port is already allocated'.

steps.prompt: Check whether another Docker container is already using port 8080.
steps.fake_output:
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE      PORTS                    NAMES
7f3a9b2c1d0e   myapp:v1   0.0.0.0:8080->3000/tcp   old-web
steps.hint: The PORTS column shows exactly which host ports each running container has claimed.

steps.prompt: The old v1 container is still holding port 8080. Stop it.
steps.hint: Stopping it frees the port, but the container still exists and can be restarted later if you need to roll back.

steps.prompt: Now start the new v2 container on port 8080.
steps.hint: The same command that failed before should work now the port is free.

steps.prompt: Clean up by removing the old stopped v1 container once you're confident v2 works.
steps.hint: Only remove it after confirming the new version is healthy — it's your quick rollback path until then.

resolution: Only one process on a host can bind a given port at a time — the old v1 container was still running and holding 8080, so the new v2 container couldn't claim it. This is the manual version of a rolling deployment: stop old, start new, confirm, then clean up. Keeping the stopped old container around until the new one is confirmed healthy is deliberate — 'docker start old-web' is an instant rollback. In a real deployment an orchestrator (Kubernetes, Compose with a load balancer) handles this handoff without any downtime window, which is exactly the problem those tools exist to solve.
